description: Composite figure combining two unlabelled panels. Top: a data table with columns "Steel", "TE/%", "YS/MPa", "UTS/MPa", "UTS × TE/MPa · %" and three rows — 0.5C: 32.8(±0.6), 614.9(±1.0), 856.7(±0.7), 28100; 0.8C: 38.4(±1.6), 711.2(±1.0), 979.1(±1.0), 37597; 1.2C: 56.2(±1.0), 735.1(±5.0), 946.7(±4.5), 53205. Bottom: a line plot of "Strain hardening rate(MPa)" (y, 0 to 4000, 500-unit ticks) versus "Strain" (x, 0.0 to 0.5, 0.1-unit ticks), with a legend giving 0.5C (black), 0.8C (red) and 1.2C (green). All three curves enter from above 4000 MPa at low strain and decay steeply; the black 0.5C curve falls fastest and plunges to zero closest to the 0.3 gridline, the red 0.8C curve collapses just beyond 0.3, and the green 1.2C curve passes through a minimum near 1700 MPa, then holds a broad plateau near 1900 MPa before dropping to zero around 0.45. Together the panels argue that higher C extends strain hardening to larger strains and thereby raises total elongation from 0.5C to 1.2C, despite 1.2C having the lowest UTS.

observations.observation: The figure group contains two different panel types: a numeric property table (top) and a line plot of strain hardening rate versus strain (bottom).
The table columns are 'Steel', 'TE/%', 'YS/MPa', 'UTS/MPa' and 'UTS × TE/MPa · %', with rows for 0.5C, 0.8C and 1.2C.
YS increases monotonically with C content (614.9 → 711.2 → 735.1 MPa), whereas UTS is highest for 0.8C (979.1 MPa) and slightly lower for 1.2C (946.7 MPa).
In the plot the y-axis is 'Strain hardening rate(MPa)' spanning 0 to 4000 with 500-unit ticks and the x-axis is 'Strain' spanning 0.0 to 0.5 with 0.1-unit ticks.
The plot legend assigns black to 0.5C, red to 0.8C and green to 1.2C.
All three strain hardening rate curves enter the plotted range from above 4000 MPa at low strain and decrease steeply, so the initial hardening rate is not resolved within the axes.
The green 1.2C curve falls to a minimum near 1700 MPa at low strain, then rises to a broad plateau near 1900 MPa that persists over a wide strain range before a final steep drop.

The strain at which the hardening rate collapses to zero increases in the order 0.5C (black, just below the 0.3 gridline) < 0.8C (red, just beyond 0.3) < 1.2C (green, midway between the 0.4 and 0.5 gridlines).
The caption labels the plot 'Variation of strain hardening rate with strain for Fe–18Mn–10Al–xC steels' and defines TE as total elongation, YS as yield strength and UTS as ultimate tensile strength.
The citing text states that 0.5C and 0.8C steels exhibit a two-stage strain hardening while 1.2C steel manifests a three-stage strain hardening.

The citing text states that 1.2C steel sustains a sufficient strain hardening rate to prevent accumulation of large strains in local regions after 0.026 strain, while 0.5C and 0.8C show decreasing strain hardening rate with true strain.
The citing text attributes the superior ductility of 1.2C steel to the more extended strain hardening rate and notes that 0.8C has higher and more extended strain hardening than 0.5C.

subfigures.description: Unlabelled table of tensile properties for 0.5C, 0.8C and 1.2C steels with columns Steel, TE/%, YS/MPa, UTS/MPa, UTS × TE/MPa · %; values with ± standard deviations are printed for each steel and the UTS × TE product rises monotonically 28100 → 37597 → 53205.

Strain hardening rate (MPa, 0-4000) versus strain (0.0-0.5) plot with legend 0.5C (black), 0.8C (red), 1.2C (green). All curves start above the top of the axis and decay; 0.5C ends at the lowest strain, 1.2C extends furthest and shows a trough then a broad plateau near 1900 MPa.

unreadable_items: Exact strain values at which each strain hardening rate curve drops to zero are not printed as labels, only readable relative to the 0.1-interval gridlines.
